title: Voetius: the honor is human and civil; one commonwealth of pilgrims and those in the homeland
source_text: XIV. Similia docet Voetius in Thesibus Theologicis. Ubi postquam posuit honorem, qui Sanctis Angelis & hominibus debetur, minime dici debere cultum Religiosum, aut servitutis, cum tantum sit cultus humanus ac civilis, immediate subjungit. Ridicula quidem Bellarmino haec appellatio videtur, sed immerito; quia & Sancti illi homines fuerunt, & una cum Angelis συμπολῖται, teste Apostolo, qui eos docet commune nobiscum πολιτευμα habere. Sed confundit Bellarminus civitatem saecularem & Ecclesiasticam, quarum illa naturae, haec gratiae est. Nam non minus hujus quam illius ratione cives unius civitatis, una Respublica, unus populus dicimur. Pars quidem in patria est, pars a patria peregrinatur, ut Apostolus loquitur; sed quantumvis illi a nobis, nos ab illis absumus, tamen & illi inter se, & nos inter nos praesentes sumus, & utrisque praesens Deus in Filio per Spiritum Sanctum. Quare cum nihil obstet quominus unius civitatis cives dicamur, nec causa quicquam erit quominus aeque civilis honor dicatur qui civibus caelestibus exhibetur, quam qui civibus terrenis: nam gradu quidem honores isti differunt, sed uterque est πολιτικός. Disput. 7. thesi 47. & seqq.
pass_a_gloss: Voetius teaches similar things in his Theological Theses. After he has set down that the honor owed to holy angels and men ought by no means to be called a religious cult, or a cult of servitude, since it is only a human and civil cult, he immediately adds: This appellation indeed seems ridiculous to Bellarmine, but undeservedly; because those Saints were men, and together with the angels fellow-citizens, as the Apostle witnesses, who teaches that they have a commonwealth in common with us. But Bellarmine confuses the secular city and the ecclesiastical, of which the former is of nature and the latter of grace. For we are called citizens of one city, one commonwealth, one people, no less by reason of this than of that. Part indeed is in the homeland, part journeys away from the homeland, as the Apostle says; but however far they are from us and we from them, yet they are present among themselves and we among ourselves, and God is present to both in the Son through the Holy Spirit. Therefore, since nothing prevents our being called citizens of one city, there will be no reason why the honor shown to heavenly citizens should not equally be called civil as that shown to earthly citizens: for those honors differ indeed in degree, but each is political. Disputation 7, thesis 47 and following.
pass_b_english: Voetius denies that honor of holy angels and people is religious cult or servitude; it is human and civil.
Against Bellarmine he notes that the Saints were human and, with the angels, fellow-citizens who share one commonwealth with us.
Bellarmine mixes the city of nature with the city of grace.
Pilgrims and those already home are one people, so honor paid to heavenly citizens is still civil, though higher in degree.

choices.why: Voetius's closing word keeps both honors inside the civil genus.
